description: Avoid seven common rotary union installation mistakes involving alignment, piping loads, filtration, thread sealing, run-in and leak testing.
h1: How to Install a Pneumatic Rotary Joint: 7 Mistakes That Cause Early Failure
h2s: Mistake 1: Installing Before Verifying the Drawing
Mistake 2: Connecting Rigid Piping Directly to the Joint

body: Home › Blog › How to Install a Pneumatic Rotary Joint: 7 Mistakes That Cause Early Failure How to Install a Pneumatic Rotary Joint: 7 Mistakes That Cause Early Failure 📅 June 11, 2026 ⏱ 10 min read 🔧 Intermediate 🌟 Begapunk Engineering Share: LinkedIn X Facebook WhatsApp Who this is for: machine builders and maintenance teams installing a pneumatic rotary joint on automation equipment, indexing tables, packaging machinery, or CNC fixtures. A rotary joint can be correctly specified and still leak or wear early if installation forces are transferred into its bearings and seals. The following checks are intentionally model-neutral. Always use the latest Begapunk drawing and the machine builder's safety procedure for final torque, clearance, filtration, and pressure-test values. Mistake 1: Installing Before Verifying the Drawing The Error The installer assumes that a similar-looking thread, flange, or port is interchangeable. Why It Causes Problems BSPP, NPT, metric, and face-seal ports use different sealing methods. A wrong thread can appear to engage while damaging the port or leaving an unreliable seal. A flange can also share the same bolt count while using a different bolt circle or locating diameter. The Fix Compare the model number, thread standard, passage layout, bolt pattern, rotating side, stationary side, and flow direction with the current drawing before assembly. Use a 3D STEP file to check surrounding clearance when space is limited. Mistake 2: Connecting Rigid Piping Directly to the Joint The Error Rigid pipe is aligned by pulling it into position and then tightened directly onto the rotary joint. Why It Causes Problems Pipe misalignment, thermal expansion, and machine vibration can place external radial or axial load on the joint. That load can disturb bearing alignment and create uneven seal contact. The Fix Support the fixed piping independently and use a compatible flexible connection where the machine design permits it. The hose must not pull, twist, or hang from the joint. Confirm pressure, temperature, bend radius, and media compatibility for the selected hose. Mistake 3: Restraining the Wrong Component The Error The rotating and stationary sides are confused, or an anti-rotation feature is clamped so rigidly that it forces the joint out of alignment. Why It Causes Problems The supply line can wind around the machine if the stationary side is allowed to rotate. Excessive restraint can create the opposite problem by transmitting frame movement into the joint. The Fix Identify the rotor and stator from the drawing. Prevent unwanted body rotation using the specified mounting feature while preserving any movement or alignment allowance stated for that model. Mistake 4: Ignoring Air and Fluid Cleanliness The Error The joint is connected to a new or recently serviced line without flushing the piping and checking the filter condition. Why It Causes Problems Metal chips, rust, sealant fragments, water, and degraded oil can damage a seal or score a running surface. The required cleanliness level depends on the medium, seal design, speed, and machine process. The Fix Flush new piping before connection, install filtration appropriate to the complete pneumatic or fluid system, and keep port plugs in place until assembly. Do not assign a universal filter rating without checking the product and process requirements. Mistake 5: Using the Wrong Thread-Sealing Method The Error PTFE tape or liquid sealant is applied to every port regardless of how that port is designed to seal. Why It Causes Problems Parallel threads may seal on a washer or O-ring, while tapered threads seal on the thread. Excess material can enter a passage and contaminate the seal. The Fix Use the sealing method specified for the exact port. Keep tape and liquid compound away from the first thread, use only media-compatible material, and remove all loose fragments before connection. Mistake 6: Starting at Full Load Without Checks The Error The machine is started immediately at production pressure and speed before rotation, port connections, and leakage are checked. Why It Causes Problems A reversed connection, external load, dry fluid circuit, or damaged fitting is harder to detect and can become more severe at full operating conditions. The Fix Use the model-specific commissioning procedure. Where the machine design allows, verify free rotation and connections first, then increase pressure and speed in controlled steps while monitoring leakage, temperature, noise, and hose movement. Mistake 7: Skipping the Final Installation Inspection The Error The machine is returned to production without documenting the installed model, operating point, leak-test result, and hose condition. Why It Causes Problems Without a baseline, later leakage or wear cannot be separated from a specification problem, installation problem, or normal service condition. The Fix Record the model and serial number, media, normal and peak pressure, RPM, temperature, mounting arrangement, filter condition, and inspection result. Photograph the final hose routing and keep the drawing with the maintenance record. Installation Checklist StepCheckEvidence 1Confirm model, rotor/stator, ports, and mounting drawingCurrent drawing or STEP file 2Inspect sealing faces, threads, O-rings, and shipping plugsNo damage or contamination 3Flush and support fixed pipingNo debris or external pipe load 4Apply the specified port-sealing methodNo excess sealant in passages 5Install mounting and anti-rotation featuresAligned with no forced fit 6Commission using approved pressure and speed stepsNo abnormal leak, heat, noise, or hose movement 7Record the final operating point and inspection resultMaintenance baseline created FAQ Why is a new rotary joint leaking immediately? Identify where the leak appears. Check thread compatibility, sealing face condition, O-ring placement, port sealant, piping load, alignment, and whether the joint rating matches the actual medium and pressure. Do not exceed the product rating during diagnosis. Should I lubricate the seal before installation? Only when the model documentation explicitly requires or permits it. Seal materials and process media react differently to lubricants, so a universal instruction is unsafe. Can I use PTFE tape and liquid sealant together? Use the single sealing method specified for the actual thread and medium. Combining materials increases the chance of contamination and does not correct a mismatched thread. What pressure should be used for the post-installation leak test? Use the pressure and duration approved for the machine and joint model. Never exceed the joint rating, isolate personnel from pressurized equipment, and follow the site's lockout and pressure-safety procedures. Conclusion The most useful installation discipline is simple: verify the drawing, prevent external loads, keep the system clean, use the correct sealing method, and document commissioning. These checks improve diagnosis and reduce avoidable rework without relying on universal torque or lifetime claims. Need an Installation Review? h1: How to Select a Pneumatic Rotary Joint: 5 Parameters That Prevent Costly Mistakes
h2s: 1. Passage Count: Match Your Pneumatic Circuit, Not Your Wish List
2. Operating Pressure: The "Max 1.0 MPa" Spec Is Misleading

body: Home › Blog › How to Select a Pneumatic Rotary Joint How to Select a Pneumatic Rotary Joint: 5 Parameters That Prevent Costly Mistakes 📅 May 24, 2026 ⏱ 8 min read 🔧 Intermediate 🌟 Begapunk Engineering Share: LinkedIn X Facebook WhatsApp A rotary joint is one of those components that either runs silently for years or stops an entire production line when it fails. The difference usually comes down to five parameters that engineers overlook during specification. Specification mismatches are an avoidable source of application problems. Operating above a model's published limits, or selecting a seal and material combination without reviewing the medium and duty, can lead to leakage or damage. Confirm the current product page and approved drawing before ordering. This guide walks through the five parameters you need to check before placing an order. Get these right, and your rotary joint will outlast the machine it is mounted on. 1. Passage Count: Match Your Pneumatic Circuit, Not Your Wish List Single-Passage, Two-Passage, and Multi-Passage Differences A 1-in-1-out rotary joint carries one medium through one rotating passage. A 2-in-2-out design carries two independent media streams through the same body — oxygen and coolant, for example, or compressed air and vacuum. Our 3-in-3-out and 4-in-4-out unions extend this logic to more complex rotary tables and indexing equipment. The critical point: each passage is mechanically isolated. A two-passage joint is not "one channel that splits in two." It is two complete seal assemblies packed into a single housing. This matters when you are counting pneumatic circuits on your machine. Common mistake: Assuming a 2-passage joint can handle mixed media without verification. If channel A carries compressed air and channel B carries cutting coolant, you need to confirm seal material compatibility for both media — not just one. How to Determine Your Passage Count Count every independent fluid path that must pass through the rotating interface: Pneumatic gripper = 2 channels (clamp + unclamp) Pneumatic gripper + vacuum ejector = 4 channels (clamp + unclamp + vacuum supply + vacuum release) Laser cutting head (clamp, unclamp, blow dust) = 3 channels Tip: If a future machine upgrade is likely, compare the cost and space of one spare passage with replacing the rotary joint later. Begapunk product reference: Single channel: BP-1P-0003 — threaded mount, compact, rated 1.0 MPa Dual channel: BP-2P-0001 — flange mount, 1.0 MPa, 6061 aluminum alloy body 2. Operating Pressure: The "Max 1.0 MPa" Spec Is Misleading Rated Pressure vs. Test Pressure When a product page or approved drawing lists "Maximum pressure: 1.0 MPa," treat that value as the model's operating limit unless the approved engineering document explicitly states otherwise. Do not use a production inspection pressure or any assumed test margin to raise the operating rating. Operating limits and production inspection conditions are separate. The current standard production leak check is performed after assembly at 1.0 MPa, with approximately 1 second of pressurization and 4 seconds of hold per passage. Any additional project-specific inspection must be agreed before order. Design rule: For continuous operation, confirm the allowable combined pressure and speed for the selected model against the current product page, approved drawing, medium, temperature, duty cycle, and installation conditions. Common mistake: Buying a 1.0 MPa joint for an application that runs at 0.9 MPa continuously. Three months later, the seal leaks. The joint did not fail — it was overspecified. Pressure Selection by Application Application Typical Pressure Recommended Begapunk Series Standard pneumatic clamping 0.3–0.6 MPa BP-1P-0003 / BP-2P-0001 High-pressure coolant delivery 0.5–2.0 MPa BP-2P-130-0001 (5.0 MPa rated) BP-2P-95-0001 reference Maximum 1.0 MPa Maximum 200 RPM; confirm medium compatibility before selection Begapunk product reference: BP-2P-0001: maximum 1.0 MPa and 200 RPM BP-2P-0002: maximum 1.0 MPa BP-2P-16-0001: maximum 200 RPM BP-2P-95-0001: maximum 1.0 MPa and 200 RPM 3. RPM: Why High Speed Needs Different Seals The Direct Relationship Between Speed and Seal Material Rotary joint seals are consumable. Their wear rate is proportional to surface speed (RPM × seal diameter). The faster the joint spins, the faster the seal material erodes. Begapunk seal material selection by speed: Speed Range Recommended Seal Max Continuous RPM < 200 RPM FKM (fluoroelastomer / Viton) 200 RPM 200–500 RPM Glyd Ring (PTFE composite) 500 RPM 500–2,000 RPM PTFE skeleton oil seal 2,000 RPM > 2,000 RPM Custom ceramic or balanced design Custom Common mistake: Selecting an FKM-sealed joint for a high-speed indexing table without reviewing pressure, speed, temperature, duty cycle, lubrication, and seal suitability. Confirm the combined operating conditions against the selected model and approved specification. At Begapunk, all high-speed models (BP-2P-95 and above) ship with PTFE skeleton oil seals as standard. We do not offer FKM on any joint rated above 200 RPM. How to Confirm Your Actual RPM Do not use the spindle's maximum RPM. Use the RPM at the joint's mounting location: A 1-second indexing cycle = 60 RPM A 0.5-second cycle = 120 RPM A continuous rotating shaft at 300 RPM = 300 RPM Most pneumatic rotary applications run well below 200 RPM. Do not overspend on a high-speed seal if your machine never breaks 100 RPM. 4. Media Compatibility: "Air" Is Not Just Air Compressed Air Has Variations Not all compressed air is the same, and the differences matter: Air Type Effect on Materials Recommended Construction Dry, filtered air Neutral Standard AL6061 + FKM/Glyd Ring Oil-fog lubricated air FKM swells, Glyd Ring resists Glyd Ring or PTFE skeleton seal mandatory Moist / unfiltered air AL6061 corrodes internally 304/316 SS body required Critical point: Moisture and contaminants in compressed air can promote internal bore corrosion in susceptible materials. The rate depends on air treatment, condensate exposure, alloy, surface treatment and operating conditions. Review filtration, drying and material selection for the actual environment. Water and Coolant Water, water-soluble coolant, and hydraulic oil require different material sets than dry air: Water / coolant → 304 SS body + Glyd Ring or EPDM seal Hydraulic oil (ISO VG 32) → 316 SS body + FKM or PTFE skeleton seal Regulated or food-contact service → document the complete wetted-material list, seal compound, cleaning chemistry, temperature, and applicable requirements before selection Common mistake: Selecting a pneumatic rotary joint for coolant without reviewing the wetted materials, seal compound, concentration, temperature, filtration, and cleaning chemistry. Confirm the complete fluid-contact configuration before selection. Begapunk product reference: Water/oil compatible (SS body): BP-2P-130-0001 Food-contact applications: request a documented review of wetted materials, seal compound, cleaning chemistry, temperature, and applicable requirements 5. Installation Space and Connection Type Threaded vs. Flange Mount Mount Type Best For Limitations Threaded (G1/8, G1/4, M5) Compact spaces, light loads Torque transfer limited; risk of loosening under vibration Flange mount High torque, high RPM, heavy hoses Requires more radial space; needs bolted face seal Rule of thumb: If the rotary joint sees significant side load from stiff hoses, or if the machine vibrates, use flange mount. The bolted connection will not loosen. At Begapunk, both mounting styles are available across most model ranges. We review your machine drawing and recommend the appropriate configuration. Size Is Not Always Smaller A smaller rotary joint does not always solve your space problem. The internal bore diameter determines flow capacity: Bore Diameter Typical Flow (air at 0.5 MPa) Suitable For 3 mm ~15 L/min Miniature grippers only 6 mm ~60 L/min Standard pneumatic cylinders 10 mm ~150 L/min Large actuators, multiple cylinders Common mistake: Buying a compact joint with a 3 mm bore to save space, then trying to run a 40 mm bore pneumatic cylinder through it. The cylinder extends slowly or stalls under load. Pressure: normal pressure, peaks, vacuum conditions and whether passages operate independently. Motion: continuous rotation, indexing or oscillation; maximum and typical speed; duty cycle. Each passage is checked separately with compressed air at 1.0 MPa while the other passages remain vented. This production inspection verifies each finished unit under the documented conditions. body: Home › Applications Air Rotary Union Applications Pneumatic rotary joints and custom air rotary unions for automation rotary tables, packaging machinery, laser cutting, CNC fixtures, bottle capping, robot tooling, pneumatic tools, vacuum packaging, welding positioners, textile printing, electronics fixtures, and dusty industrial equipment. Find a Suitable Rotary Union Request Engineering Support Application-Driven Selection Built Around Real Machine Requirements Begapunk helps machine builders, OEM engineers, and distributors select air rotary unions based on passage count, pressure, RPM, mounting method, air quality, and installation environment. Instead of choosing only by model number, engineers can start from the machine function: clamping, unclamping, blow-off, vacuum, indexing, rotating fixture supply, or protected pneumatic transfer in dusty environments. Common selection inputs Number of independent air passages Maximum pressure and rotational speed Mounting space, flange pattern, or thread type Compressed air quality and filtration Need for 2D drawing or 3D CAD review Applications Where Begapunk Air Rotary Unions Are Used Start from your machine type, then match the passage count, mounting method, and protection level. Automation Rotary Tables Rotary indexing tables in automation lines need continuous air supply to pneumatic clamps, vacuum ejectors, and blow-off nozzles while rotating 360°. A failed rotary joint stops the entire indexing cycle and scrapes the production batch. Typical requirement: 2–4 independent air passages at 0.3–0.6 MPa, 60–120 RPM indexing speed, with flange mount for anti-rotation stability. Multi-passage layouts provide separate flow paths for clamp and vacuum circuits; confirm the required cross-port leakage limit for the selected configuration. Typical air functions Clamping, unclamping, blow-off, vacuum holding, sensor air. Recommended products BP-2P-0001 (2-passage flange), BP-3P-0004 (3-passage), BP-4P-30-0001 (4-passage, 30mm bore), BP-8P-0001 (8-passage high-channel). View Application Packaging Machinery Rotary packaging machines — pouch fillers, form-fill-seal lines, and rotary sealers — need compact air transfer in tight machine envelopes. Select the rotary union around passage functions, installation space, cleaning method, and service access. Typical requirement: 1–3 passages at 0.4–0.8 MPa, compact threaded mount for tight turret envelopes, with quick-disconnect fittings for fast maintenance changeout. Review stainless steel body options, washdown conditions, and required food or pharmaceutical documentation for the selected configuration. Typical air functions Sealing head actuation, indexing control, vacuum release, film tension. Recommended products BP-1P-0003 (compact single-passage), BP-2P-0001 (2-passage flange), BP-3P-0004 (3-passage compact), custom layouts for OEM integration. View Application Laser tube cutting machine rear chucks These standard-model applications transfer compressed air between the stationary supply and the rotating rear chuck. Process or assist-gas transfer is handled as a separate engineering project with application-specific materials, cleaning, testing, and approval. Verified scope Rear-chuck compressed-air transfer. Confirm circuit count, port functions, and interfaces against the chuck and machine design. Standard models for rear-chuck compressed air BP-3P-0004 and BP-2P-08-0001. Select the passage count and interfaces from the chuck and machine design. View Application CNC Fixtures and Pneumatic Clamping CNC rotary tables and 4th-axis fixtures rely on stable pneumatic clamping pressure to hold workpieces during machining. Pressure drop during rotation causes clamp release — and a destroyed workpiece or broken tool. Repeatable clamping force is non-negotiable. Typical requirement: 2–3 passages at 0.3–0.6 MPa, flange mount for rigid fixture integration, with through-bore options for coolant or wiring passage. Confirm the continuous-duty pressure and speed for the selected model against the current product page, approved drawing, medium, temperature, and clamping cycle. Typical air functions Fixture clamping, unclamping, pressure holding, rotary table air supply, coolant through-bore. Recommended products BP-2P-0001 (clamp + unclamp), BP-3P-0004 (3-passage flange), BP-4P-30-0001 (4-passage with 30mm through-bore), custom for coolant integration. View Application Bottle Filling and Capping Machines Rotary filling turrets and capping heads in beverage and pharmaceutical lines rotate at 60–200 RPM while controlling pneumatic torque, vacuum hold-down, and bottle gripper actuation. A leak at the rotary joint causes inconsistent fill levels or loose caps — both are rejected product. Typical requirement: Review passage count, pressure, mounting envelope, wetted materials, cleaning chemistry, and applicable food-contact or regulatory requirements for the selected configuration. Agree the required documentation before ordering. Typical air functions Filling head actuation, capping torque control, vacuum bottle hold-down, gripper air, washdown blow-off. Models to review BP-1P-0003 (compact single-passage), BP-2P-0001 (2-passage), and BP-3P-0004 (3-passage compact). Final materials and applicable compliance documentation are established through a documented configuration review. View Application Robot End-of-Arm Tooling (EOAT) Robot grippers, suction cups, and rotating wrists need air and vacuum transfer through a compact rotary joint at the end of the arm. Weight and size are critical — every gram at the EOAT reduces payload capacity. A failed joint means dropped parts and production line stops. Typical requirement: 2–3 passages at 0.3–0.6 MPa, ultra-compact threaded mount (often M5 or G1/8), lightweight 6061 aluminum alloy body, with integrated electrical slip ring options for combined pneumatic-electric EOAT designs. Typical air functions Gripper clamp/unclamp, vacuum suction, blow-off release, tool changer actuation, sensor air. Recommended products BP-1P-0003 (ultra-compact), BP-2P-0002 (2-passage G1/8), BP-3P-S06-0001 (3-passage + 6 electrical circuits), custom EOAT layouts. View Application Pneumatic Tools and Hose Anti-Twist Handheld pneumatic tools — tightening guns, grinders, sanders — can twist the air hose with every rotation. A compact air swivel at the tool inlet helps prevent kinks, airflow restriction, and fatigue at the fitting. Typical requirement: Single passage at 0.4–0.8 MPa, threaded mount (G1/4 or G1/8), compact body for handheld tool integration, with 360° free rotation and low torque drag so the operator does not feel resistance. Typical air functions Tool inlet air supply, hose strain relief, anti-twist 360° rotation. Recommended products BP-1P-0003 (G1/4, compact), BP-1P-0006 (1-in-6-out, G1/8, 4mm orifice), BP-2P-0002 (dual passage for tool + exhaust). View Application Vacuum Packaging Machines Rotary vacuum packaging turrets need simultaneous vacuum extraction and release air on independent channels. Cross-contamination between vacuum and compressed air destroys package seal integrity. Each passage should be specified with an application-appropriate isolation and allowable cross-port leakage criterion. Confirm the channel-isolation test conditions and acceptance limits for the selected model. Typical requirement: 2–3 passages (vacuum + release air + clamp), 0.05–0.1 MPa vacuum side / 0.4–0.6 MPa air side, 60–120 RPM turret speed, with flange mount for rigid turret integration. Review seal materials and required food-contact documentation for the selected configuration. Typical air functions Vacuum extraction, release air, clamp actuation, sealing bar air, pouch gripper vacuum. Recommended products BP-2P-0001 (vacuum + air), BP-3P-0004 (3-passage), BP-3P-0006 (G1/4 multi-line), custom air/vacuum isolated layouts. View Application Welding Positioners and Pipe Rotators Rotary welding tables and pipe rotators operate around weld spatter, grinding dust, and vibration. Dust ingress and side loads can accelerate wear, so shielding, bearing protection, hose routing, and external loads should be reviewed for the actual installation. Typical requirement: Confirm passage count, pressure, speed, mounting, material, weld-spatter exposure, vibration, and the required ingress-protection level from the machine specification. Match the shielding and external protection to the actual installation. Typical air functions Fixture clamping, unclamping, blow-off spatter removal, shielding gas support, positioner brake air. Recommended products BP-2P-50-0001 (protective shroud and labyrinth for dusty environments), BP-3P-0004 (3-passage flange), BP-4P-30-0001 (4-passage heavy-duty), custom protected layouts with weld spatter shields. View Application Textile, Printing, and Converting Rotating rollers, winding shafts, and printing drums need air blow-off, vacuum web handling, and sometimes coolant or water transfer. Paper dust and textile fibers are abrasive contaminants that score standard seals. Filtration and seal material selection are critical for 24/7 converting lines. Typical requirement: 1–2 passages at 0.2–0.5 MPa, 100–500 RPM continuous rotation, through-bore for shaft passage, with 10-micron filtration and PTFE seals for fiber resistance. Water-compatible stainless steel body for coolant applications. Typical air functions Web blow-off, vacuum web holding, roller cooling, tension control air, edge trim vacuum. View Application Electronics and Battery Test Fixtures Rotating test fixtures for batteries, PCBs, and semiconductor components need precise pneumatic clamping and vacuum holding during inspection. ESD-sensitive environments require clean, dry air with no oil contamination. Compact size is critical — test fixtures often have <50 mm clearance around the rotation axis. Typical requirement: 2–3 passages at 0.1–0.4 MPa, 60–300 RPM, ultra-compact threaded mount (M5 or G1/8), with oil-free PTFE seals and optional integrated electrical circuits for signal transfer alongside pneumatic lines. Typical air functions Test fixture clamping, vacuum component holding, blow-off debris removal, probe actuation, ESD-safe air supply. Recommended products BP-1P-0003 (ultra-compact), BP-2P-0002 (G1/8 dual), BP-3P-S06-0001 (3-passage + 6 electrical circuits), custom pneumatic-electric integrated designs. View Application Steel Mills and Dusty Industrial Environments Steel mills, foundries, cement plants, and mining equipment can expose rotary joints to abrasive dust, metal chips, and vibration. Review contamination, shielding, mounting, and maintenance together; a protective shroud and labyrinth can reduce direct exposure. Typical requirement: Confirm passage count, pressure, speed, mounting, body material, filtration, contamination type, shielding, vibration, and the required ingress-protection level. Select the protective configuration from the actual machine environment. Typical air functions Pneumatic clamping in dusty environments, blow-off debris removal, actuator control, conveyor brake air, protected tool air supply. Begapunk manufactures single-passage and multi-passage rotary unions for industrial automation, CNC machining, laser cutting, packaging, and other rotating machinery applications. What is the difference between a rotary joint and a rotary union? ▼ There is no technical difference — the terms are used interchangeably in the industry. title: Rotary Joint Installation Instructions | Begapunk Support
description: Step-by-step installation guide for Begapunk rotary joints and rotary unions. Proper mounting, connections, anti-rotation, filtration, and maintenance.
h1: Installation Instructions
body: Home / Installation Instructions Installation Instructions Proper mounting, connection, and maintenance guidelines for Begapunk rotary joints and rotary unions. Follow these steps to support reliable operation and reduce avoidable leakage risk. 1 Connections 1Use flexible connections. Begapunk rotary joints must always be installed using flexible hose connections. To avoid damage to the bearings, the union needs to find its center during operation. Never hard-pipe either the shaft or the housing. 2Pre-assemble in a vise. Hold the housing of the union in a vise and install the flexible connection before mounting the union to the machine. This prevents twisting during installation. 3Clean and seal threads. Clean female threads and the face of the shaft prior to installation. Use PTFE (Teflon) pipe tape or pipe sealant on NPT threads. NPT threads should be hand-tight plus 1–3 turns to seal. For parallel threads, use appropriate gaskets or O-rings. 4Allow free movement. There should be a slight, kink-free curve in the hose when installed. It is essential that the housing or shaft is allowed to float to compensate for any eccentricity or misalignment. Important: Hard-piping either side will transfer machine vibration and misalignment directly to the bearings and seals, causing premature failure. 2 Anti-Rotation In many applications, the flexible hose connections themselves provide sufficient anti-rotation. For other installations, an external anti-rotation device is required — such as a fork around the fittings, pin, yoke, or bracket. Anti-rotation devices must "float." They should prevent rotation of the stationary side but must not rigidly lock the union in place. The device must allow the union to self-center during operation. Warning: A rigid anti-rotation setup that prevents the union from accommodating permitted movement can transfer misalignment or side load into the seal and bearing. Follow the clearance and support requirements in the approved installation instructions. 3 Filtration To prevent scoring damage to the shaft and seal faces, Begapunk requires fluid filtration to 25 microns or finer for general applications, and 10 microns or finer for high-speed or precision unions. Contaminants larger than the seal gap will embed in the seal material and grind grooves into the shaft face. This damage is irreversible and will cause progressive leakage. Warranty Note: Failure to provide adequate filtration may void your warranty and cause premature failure. 4 Lubrication If your Begapunk rotary joint is equipped with grease fittings (typically on the bearing housing): Use lithium-based grease rated for the operating temperature of your application. Lubricate with no more than two pumps of grease per fitting during routine maintenance. Over-greasing can force grease past the seals and contaminate the fluid path. Refer to your product data sheet for the recommended lubrication interval (typically every 3–6 months for continuous-duty applications). 5 Startup Checklist Verify all connections are tight but not over-torqued. Confirm hoses have a gentle curve — no tension or kinks. Check that the anti-rotation device allows free float. Verify filtration system is active and filter is clean. Start at low speed and pressure, then gradually ramp to operating conditions. Inspect for leaks during the first 30 minutes of operation. 6 Maintenance Monthly: Visual inspection for leaks, hose condition, and anti-rotation clearance. Quarterly: Grease bearings (if fitted), check filter pressure differential, inspect seal faces for wear. Annually: Replace seals if leakage exceeds acceptable limits. Contact Begapunk for OEM seal kits — third-party seals may have incorrect durometer or material. Need a seal kit or have questions? Contact our support team with your product serial number.
